reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard haematology references
clinicalPearls: An inherited bone marrow failure syndrome caused by defects in the Fanconi anaemia DNA-repair pathway, leading to chromosomal instability
Progressive pancytopenia usually emerges in the first decade, often beginning with thrombocytopenia or macrocytosis with a raised fetal haemoglobin
Congenital anomalies are common but not universal, including short stature, abnormal thumbs and radii, cafe-au-lait spots, microcephaly, and renal or genitourinary malformations
The diagnostic hallmark is increased chromosomal breakage in lymphocytes exposed to DNA cross-linking agents such as diepoxybutane or mitomycin C
Patients carry a markedly increased lifetime risk of myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myeloid leukaemia, and solid tumours, notably head and neck and gynaecological squamous cancers
Most cases are autosomal recessive, with a smaller number X-linked; many complementation groups and genes are recognised

Management principles include haematological support, androgens to improve counts in some patients, and allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the definitive treatment for marrow failure
Patients are exquisitely sensitive to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, so conditioning and cancer treatment must be substantially modified to avoid excessive toxicity
Lifelong cancer surveillance and screening of siblings and potential related donors are essential
reference.pathophysiology: Fanconi anaemia is caused by biallelic (or, in one gene, X-linked) mutations in any of numerous genes encoding proteins of the Fanconi anaemia/BRCA DNA-repair pathway. This pathway repairs interstrand DNA cross-links and maintains genomic stability during replication. Defective repair leads to accumulation of DNA damage, increased apoptosis of haematopoietic stem cells, and progressive bone marrow failure, together with heightened chromosomal fragility. The same genomic instability underlies the strong predisposition to myelodysplasia, acute myeloid leukaemia and epithelial malignancies, and explains the marked hypersensitivity of cells to DNA-damaging agents.
additionalDifferentials: Other inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, Diamond-Blackfan anaemia)
Thrombocytopenia-absent radius (TAR) syndrome and other congenital anomaly syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal breakage testing with diepoxybutane or mitomycin C (the confirmatory test)
Full blood count and blood film with fetal haemoglobin level
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics to assess cellularity and evolving clonal change
Molecular genetic testing to identify the causative gene and complementation group
Baseline and surveillance imaging and endoscopy for associated malignancies and organ anomalies
redFlags: Progressive or severe pancytopenia indicating marrow failure requiring urgent haematology input
New cytogenetic clonal abnormalities or blasts signalling transformation to MDS or acute leukaemia
Development of head and neck, oesophageal or gynaecological squamous carcinoma
Severe, unexpected toxicity from standard-dose chemotherapy or radiotherapy
Life-threatening infection or bleeding from severe cytopenia
reference.prognosis: Untreated, progressive marrow failure and a high risk of leukaemic transformation and solid tumours limit survival. Allogeneic stem cell transplantation can correct the haematological disease, but does not remove the elevated solid-tumour risk, so lifelong cancer surveillance remains necessary; overall outlook depends on the specific genotype, timing of transplant and emergence of malignancy.
pitfalls: Treating apparent aplastic anaemia without excluding Fanconi anaemia, risking catastrophic transplant conditioning toxicity
Giving standard-dose chemotherapy or radiotherapy to which patients are hypersensitive
Overlooking the diagnosis in adults or in those without congenital anomalies
Using a related donor for transplant without screening them for the same disorder
Neglecting long-term malignancy surveillance after successful transplant
